paraphrase: Voluntary guidance sets out a structured approach to pre-deployment testing of LLM apps, from outputs to components, to ascertain baseline safety and reliability before going live.
what_is_tested: LLM app baseline safety and reliability
notes: Whole document is voluntary guidance; five risks in scope

locator: 1.1.1 What does the Starter Kit do, p.9
paraphrase: Three step approach: identify relevant risks, run tests in a structured way from outputs to components, then assess results against baseline safety.
what_is_tested: app outputs and components against identified risks

paraphrase: Developers and testers can use the guide to validate whether the app is safe and reliable; compliance staff can use it to judge sufficiency of testing.
Kit focuses on the pre-deployment testing phase of the software life cycle, to check the app meets baseline requirements before deployment.
notes: Post-deployment monitoring noted as essential but out of scope (fn 2)

paraphrase: Kit is aligned with AI Verify outcomes that recommend regular safety testing and testing for potential bias, and with NIST AI RMF MEASURE functions.
Testing phase of the life cycle is to verify performance and safety; kit complements and does not replace standard unit, integration and system testing.
Baseline is achieved when test results show the app meets safety thresholds; each organisation must set its own threshold before the app goes into production.
notes: Uses 'must' but inside voluntary guidance, so non_binding

paraphrase: Organisations can use curated public core benchmarks per risk (some in Project Moonshot, some in development) if representative and well designed, and check for the latest version.
notes: Alternatives named while Singapore benchmark in development (fn 5-7)

paraphrase: Test methodology must be rigorous and well designed for results to be credible; approach should combine output testing and component testing, via benchmarking and red teaming.
Output testing treats the app as a black box, evaluates it as a whole as end users would, to surface issues before release, and may be repeated until thresholds are met.
Component testing inside the pipeline identifies failure points and hidden issues, by testing a component in isolation or comparing the system with and without it.
Pre-deployment testing may also include user testing such as simulation, pilots and A/B testing.
Results should be robust and consistent: use varied test sets and multiple runs, even on a subset, to detect unstable outcomes.
what_is_tested: stability of test results across runs

paraphrase: Testing methods should be rigorous so that test results are valid and trusted.
Benchmarking presents standard prompts, compares responses to reference answers and scores them; well designed benchmarks address many central concerns.
Benchmarks need to be complemented by red teaming for blind spots, rare failure modes and multi-turn scenarios; simulation based testing may also be considered.
notes: Footnote 13 gives sample size arithmetic (about 10,000 prompts for 0.01% failure rate at 99.99% confidence)

paraphrase: Test dataset should represent the app's purpose, domain and anticipated usage, with realistic inputs, subject matter expert input, and about 30-50 prompts per narrow topic (100-200 wider).
Metrics should align with test objectives, dataset format and business or policy goals; own metric or acceptability rules may be defined when no reference answer exists.
Automated evaluators (rule based, LLM-as-a-Judge, fine tuned) should supplement not replace expert human judgement; human experts should check a smaller sample.
notes: One passage says human check is crucial

paraphrase: Users can switch evaluators or define their own LLM-as-a-Judge criteria in the testing tool.
Red teaming dynamically probes the app for weaknesses, can complement benchmarking by stress testing, and can serve as an alternative evaluation method.
what_is_tested: app weaknesses under adversarial or benign probing

paraphrase: Clarify red teaming objectives at the outset, define a risk taxonomy, choose a representative and diverse composition of red teamers.
Scoring should be simple, human review and sampling of LLM judge annotations is encouraged, and organisations should protect red teamers from distressing material.
IMDA ran a multicultural, multilingual red teaming exercise across nine countries.
notes: Description of practice, not pre-deployment of a specific product

paraphrase: Automated red teaming uses an attacker LLM to iteratively probe and refine attacks; a case study tested an agency chatbot across priority behaviour categories.
Testing is not a one-off exercise; revisit risk assessment and repeat relevant tests when the app changes.
Prioritise testing the risks that matter most, via top down down-selection or bottom up usage scenarios, with an optional likelihood and severity matrix.
Test depth should reflect reputational or legal exposure; even low risk apps should run simple tests on a small representative set; repeat tests and report average, minimum and maximum.
Each organisation must set its own thresholds before testing, with clear targets per risk scenario, refined and validated after testing.
For illegal or high stakes harms the benchmark threshold should be zero failures, with retesting until met, and organisations should keep up to date with regulations.

Thresholds can be set relative to human performance, peer apps, base model or prior version; developers should ensure the app is at least as safe as its base model; quick sample tests can inform thresholds.
Case study used a default 95% safe response threshold and treated any failure on hard gate topics as requiring investigation and mitigation.
Recommends testing the app in two areas: domain specific knowledge and out of domain topics.
Test accuracy by comparing output with expected output, or test grounding when no expected output exists, preferably with a custom dataset built from the knowledge base.
Match methods range from exact match to semantic similarity; long outputs can be split into claims and evaluated; precision or completeness may be prioritised.
A RAG assistant was tested with multiple metrics plus domain expert review.
For summarisation apps create a custom dataset of typical sources, test grounding of each summary statement and completeness, and optionally conciseness.
Case study used ROUGE, FactScore and human evaluation as a final check.
Test that out of domain questions are declined or routed to a fallback, using the benchmark approach, LLM-as-a-Judge for refusals, and red teaming near the refusal boundary.
what_is_tested: refusal of out of domain queries

paraphrase: Developers can use an open tool to build out of knowledge base robustness tests for their RAG pipeline.
Component tests should target two failure points: retrieval of relevant information and grounding of generated output in what was retrieved.
Isolate the retriever and compare retrieved items to ground truth using precision and recall (recall first), or an LLM judge for relevance when no ground truth exists; keep references current.
Test whether output is grounded in retrieved information using a binary or percentage grounding score from a fine tuned model or LLM judge, reusing the output test dataset.
Case study tested an AML summariser with 400 multilingual samples including perturbed inputs, measuring precision of extracted facts.
Test for bias by checking protected characteristics do not influence outcomes, using parity testing (group error rates) and/or perturbation testing (change one attribute at a time).
Pick parity testing when groups and ground truth labels exist; perturbation testing when labels are unavailable or for specific updates.

locator: 3.3.1 Parity testing dataset and steps, p.54-55
paraphrase: Build a balanced representative dataset of decision cases with sufficient samples per group and a correct outcome label per case, run it, derive parity metrics.
what_is_tested: group parity of accuracy and errors
notes: Source text uses 'must' for outcome labels; text available ends mid-sentence on p.55 before the test administration step
